messages.subject: Is DISTANCE-SAMPLING appropriate for these data?
parts:
I am new to DISTANCE-SAMPLING and need to know if it can used with our ex=
isting data set.


We have data from helicopter surveys of flushing birds. The transects we=
re 200m wide (e.g., 100m off each side of the helicopter). The helicopte=
r was flown at an altitude of 4 meters (observor'e eye-levels at 5 meters=
).

Observors recorded all the birds within the transect boundaries, ahead of=
, under and to the side of the aircraft, BUT DID NOT RECORD DISTANCES OR =
THE SIGHT-ANGLES TO EACH BIRD.

It has been suggested by some that calibration surveys can be flown after=
-the-fact to get bird sighting detection functions (probability) for unde=
r the helicopter and for the probability of sighting birds at varying dis=
tances to the side to allow the use of the DISTANCE-SAMPLING program to a=
nalyze our old data for population density determination. We can fly the=
same locations in the same way at the same time of the year. How this i=
s possible is not clear to me.

If this is not possible without actual distances observed for each bird s=
ighting, is there another suitable analysis tool we can use to estimate d=
ensities from these data?

Many thanks for comments/advice.

messages.author: dc8b4131b39a099f
messages.subject: Re: Is DISTANCE-SAMPLING appropriate for these data?
parts:
Hi Buddy. I couldn't tell from your email, but if you have temporally
repeated sampling visits to your sites, say within a nesting season or
period of time during which you can reasonably assume the population was
closed, then you can use Royle's 2004 N-mixture model for
abundance/density. The model is available in Program PRESENCE and unmarked
for R (http://sites.google.com/site/unmarkedinfo/home). Alternatively, if
you suspect the pop closure assumption was violated, you can use Dail and
Madsen's open N-mixture model, also available in unmarked for R. Best,

Matt

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Is DISTANCE-SAMPLING appropriate for these data?
parts:
Hi Buddy,

Yes, I think this will work, if you're willing to assume that the
detection function from the calibration surveys applies to your original
surveys -- this is an assumption you can't test.

How do you do the analysis? Do would do a standard detection function
modelling analysis of the distances from the calibration survey and use
this to get an estimated P (average probability of detection between
distance 0 and the truncation distance), SE on P and DF on P. You'd
then enter these into Distance as multipliers. Lastly, you'd run an
analysis on the original survey where, instead of fitting a detection
function (under detection function you specify a uniform key function
and 0 adjustment terms), you'd use the P, SE(P) and df from the
calibration survey. This kind of thing is described under "Multipliers"
in the Distance help, although not exactly in this context.

Hope this helps,

- Len Thomas

--

parts:
Buddy & Matt
Royle's 2004 N-mixture model is among several conventional methods for dete=
ctability that give very biased estimates in the presence of individual het=
erogeneity, and distance-related individual heterogeneity is inevitable in=
point and line-transect samples. Efford & Dawson (2009 Auk 126: 100-111) d=
ocumented this for point counts. Distance-related heterogeneity is likely t=
o be less with transect sampling, but there will be heterogeneity from othe=
r sources. If you really need to estimate density then I think in this case=
double-sampling (calibration) is the serious option.
Murray Efford

messages.author: dc8b4131b39a099f
messages.subject: Re: Is DISTANCE-SAMPLING appropriate for these data?
parts:
Murray makes a good point regarding distance effects on point counts and
models based on temporally replicated visits, and Efford and Dawson's 2009
Auk paper is a useful accomplishment indeed. Nonetheless, N-mixture and
related MLE models have been and continue to be useful tools for

understanding relationships between relative abundance/density and habitat
and landscape features. I guess Buddy's decision could be influenced by
whether his goal is solely to estimate population size (perhaps among years
or sites) or to investigate why population size varies. Regardless, I
certainly wouldn't dismiss entire suites of modeling approaches based on the

conclusions of a single research simulation.

I agree with Len and Murray that resampling for sake of estimating a
detection function is reasonable, especially if you can use the same

observers and qualify that the factors influencing detection haven't changed
much over time. But my original point is that if you have data based on
temporally repeated visits, then you have a set of rigorous modeling tools

available that might complement your data, without having to invest the
likely significant resources in resampling. Best,

Matt

messages.author: 6e15de0134e98c08
messages.subject: Re: Is DISTANCE-SAMPLING appropriate for these data?
parts:
Hi Matt, all

I guess the question boils down to what are the assumptions underlying=20
the "rigorous modelling tools" you are referring to.

It is not enough that the modelling tool is rigorous, you also need that=20
the underlying assumptions of a rigorous method hold to a reasonable=20
extent in the practical example at hand.

What the Efford and Dawson's 2009 Auk paper showed is something which is=20
essentially intuitive. If there is a fair amount of unmodeled=20
heterogeneity which is not accounted for in your model, in particular=20
from distance from the transect (which is likely the case in Buddy's=20
study, given his description), then the N-mixture model (and others)=20
might not be ideal and lead to considerable bias. So in the case at=20
hand, it seems like the N-mixture model could indeed lead to=20
considerable bias. So while I agree with you that one should not dismiss=20
entire suites of modeling approaches based on a single study, I think=20
one might want to dismiss said entire suit of modelling approaches under=20
those scenarios where the corresponding assumptions do not hold. That=20
will be valid for any modelling approach.

Note that the assumption that the detection function is the same in the=20
survey and in the calibration study will be however a leap of faith, yet=20
one that people often make. Assessing whether factors that might have=20
changed (like observers, or weather conditions, or helicopter type, say)=20
have a strong influence in the detection function might be a way to test=20
to what extent you might be going wrong if you take the calibration route.

Cheers,

T.

messages.subject: Re: Is DISTANCE-SAMPLING appropriate for these data?
parts:
Hi Tiago-

Greetings from the other side of the planet. I couldn't agree more that
assessing assumptions of models is critical (especially given the
constraints of data already sampled), which is exactly why I highlighted th=
e
primary assumption of mixture models based on temporally replicated visits
in my first response to Buddy's inquiry. I further suggested an alternativ=
e
mixture model (Dail and Madsen 2011) for when closure is unlikely.

I disagree, however, that assessing assumptions is the sole or even primary
criteria with which to make a decision in this case because understanding
the research goal (which I admittedly do not) is equally as important. If
the goal is to simply estimate absolute abundance of some population,
without modeling it as a function of ecological variables, then Efford and
Dawson's (2009) simulations suggest that the N-mixture model may not be
ideal. If the goal, however, is to model relative abundance as a function
of some variables representing, for example, landscape configuration or
habitat structure, then mixture models based on temporally replicated visit=
s
might be suitable.

Best,

Matt
* *___
Matt Giovanni, Ph.D.
Research Wildlife Ecologist
402-617-3764 mobile

http://sites.google.com/site/matthewgiovanni/

e

> >
> > It is not enough that the modelling tool is rigorous, you also need that
> > the underlying assumptions of a rigorous method hold to a reasonable exte=

nt
> > in the practical example at hand.
> >

> > What the Efford and Dawson's 2009 Auk paper showed is something which is
> > essentially intuitive. If there is a fair amount of unmodeled heterogenei=
ty
> > which is not accounted for in your model, in particular from distance fro=
m
> > the transect (which is likely the case in Buddy's study, given his
> > description), then the N-mixture model (and others) might not be ideal an=
d
> > lead to considerable bias. So in the case at hand, it seems like the
> > N-mixture model could indeed lead to considerable bias. So while I agree
> > with you that one should not dismiss entire suites of modeling approaches
> > based on a single study, I think one might want to dismiss said entire su=
it
> > of modelling approaches under those scenarios where the corresponding
> > assumptions do not hold. That will be valid for any modelling approach.

> >
> > Note that the assumption that the detection function is the same in the
> > survey and in the calibration study will be however a leap of faith, yet =

one
> > that people often make. Assessing whether factors that might have changed
> > (like observers, or weather conditions, or helicopter type, say) have a
> > strong influence in the detection function might be a way to test to what

> > extent you might be going wrong if you take the calibration route.

Friends,

Interesting though it is, can I ask for you to stop posting on this
thread now. The distance-sampling list is not intended as a discussion
list or forum; rather a low-volume "question and answer" style email
list. If there are too many posts, people will leave. Feel free,
however, to continue the discussion off the list, and post a summary of
your deliberations to the list in due course, as a single message.
Thanks again,

- Len Thomas (distance-sampling list admin)

file that all users get when they join the list

Copy of distance-sampling.welcome file:

************************************
* DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK *
************************************

PLEASE SAVE THIS MESSAGE FOR FUTURE REFERENCE,
IT CONTAINS VITAL INFORMATION

Welcome to the DISTANCE SAMPLING e-mail discussion list. The purpose of
this list is to promote the sharing of ideas and information among
researchers and practitioners interested in distance sampling techniques
(see below). Suitable topics for postings include:

o Questions about distance sampling survey design and analysis.
o New methodological developments in distance sampling.
o Use of software tools (program DISTANCE and other software).
o News about up-coming meetings, workshops and conferences where
distance methods will be discussed.
o Jobs in distance sampling fields.

Instructions for subscribing, unsubscribing, posting and getting help
are given in subsequent sections.

Before posting any messages,

** PLEASE READ THE LIST GUIDELINES **

which are given near the end of this file. Very briefly the key points
are:

o Make sure distance-sampling is the appropriate forum for your message.
If you are unsure ask the list owner first.
o Use informative subject lines.
o If seeking a reply, include your address in the body of your message.
Offer to compile the replies you recieve and summarize them to
the list.
o If replying, consider whether to reply to the sender rather than
the list.
o Send plain text only (no Word or encoded files or other attachments).
o Do not post commercial advertising (however announcements about
jobs, conferences, non-commercial software, etc are okay).


========================================================================
Background
========================================================================

Distance sampling is a widely used technique for estimating the abundance
of biological populations. Distance sampling methods include line
transects, point transects (variable circular plots), cue counting,
trapping webs and migration counts. An introduction to the the
methods is given in the following book:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers, D.L,
and Thomas, L. (2001). Introduction to Distance Sampling. Oxford University
Press, Oxford, UK.

A previous edition of the book is freely available for download on the
internet
at http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

Recent methodological developments and applications are also discussed in
biological journals such as the Journal of Wildlife Management, Ecology,
Biometrics, and the Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Ecological
Statistics.

The standard software for the design and analysis of distance sampling
data is program Distance. Newer versions are fully windows-based with an
intuitive point-and-click interface. The software is freely available for
download from the Distance home page
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/


========================================================================
Important Email Addresses
========================================================================

1. distance...@jiscmail.ac.uk

This is the address of this list. Any messages sent to this address
will be automatically forwarded to all the members of the list.

2. jisc...@jiscmail.ac.uk

This is the JISCmail program. You send commands (such as
join distance-sampling) to this address.

3. distance-sam...@jiscmail.ac.uk

This is the address for the list owner who looks after the list
(currently Len Thomas of the University of St Andrews, UK).

If you have a problem with the list, send a message to this address.

For example,
- if you have problems leaving the list
- if you have problems sending a message to the list

4. jiscmail...@jiscmail.ac.uk

This is the JISCmail Helpline.
If you have any questions about or problems with the JISCmail system
use this address.


========================================================================
Important World-Wide Web sites
========================================================================

1. http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling.html

This is the list home page. Here you will find information about
the list (this file), an archive of all messages to the list over the
past year, and other files that I may post from time to time.

2. http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk

JISCmail home page. From here you can find out more about how to
manage your list membership, and about the other lists run by the
JISCmail server.


========================================================================
How to...
========================================================================

1. To send a message to everyone on the list, send an email to:
distance...@jiscmail.ac.uk

2. To leave distance-sampling, send an email to:
jisc...@jiscmail.ac.uk
with the message:
leave distance-sampling
--

3. To join distance-sampling, send an email to:
jisc...@jiscmail.ac.uk
with the message:
join distance-sampling yourfirstname yourlastname
--
Replace the text "yourfirstname" with your first name and the text
"yourlastname" with your last name
(e.g., join distance-sampling Joan Smith)

4. To find out more about what the JISCmail server can do (for example
searching the monthly archive of messages, suspending mail when you're
on holiday, etc):
a) Check out the web pages at http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk especially
http://jiscmail.ac.uk/docs/user-ref-card.html
b) Send an e-mail to:
jisc...@jiscmail.ac.uk
with the message:
info
